newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian socialist party crumbles, clings to power.
newsitem.headline: Belgian socialist party crumbles, clings to power.

text.p: Belgium's scandal-ridden Socialist Party (PS) is visibly crumbling but has no intention of giving up its seat in the country's four-party centre-left coalition, government sources said on Thursday.

"The PS is a virtual party now. Its substance has gone and will have to be rebuilt from the base up. But it will not move into opposition just now," one Belgian government source said on condition of anonymity.

Three senior party officials -- Merry Hermanus, Francois Pirot and Fernand Detaille -- are in jail and under investigation over 45 million Belgian francs ($1.3 million) in bribes alleged to have been paid by French avionics firm Dassault in the late 1980s to win a large defence contract.
Dassault, whose chief Serge Dassault is the subject of an international arrest warrant issued by Belgium, has denied any wrongdoing.

Guy Spitaels, chairman of the Francophone PS at the time, also denies all knowledge of the money but on Thursday finally gave in to intense political pressure and resigned from the parliament of the country's French-speaking Walloon region.

He had already temporarily stepped down from the presidency of the assembly -- one of four regional parliaments in linguistically divided Belgium -- while the allegations that he knew of the bribes are investigated.

Former party treasurer Patrick Moriau, whose name is on one of the three bank accounts at Union Bank of Switzerland's Luxembourg branch which prosecutors say were used to launder the funds, will have his parliamentary immunity from prosecution lifted on Thursday.
And the fingers of blame are increasingly pointing at current PS chairman Philippe Bousquin who likewise denies all knowledge of the money or the accounts.
Bousquin faces re-election to the PS chair this weekend.

The bribery allegations, similar to those concerning Italian helicopter maker Agusta which forced NATO Secretary General Willy Claes, a Flemish Socialist, to resign 18 months ago, have prompted opposition calls for the PS to quit the coalition.

The calls have been rejected -- not least by Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, a Flemish Christian Democrat, who has fought behind the scenes to keep his government intact while it bids to make the economy fit to join the European Union's single currency.
The EU will decide early next year which countries will make the grade at the start of 1999 -- the year in which, coincidentally, the next national elections are due.
Diplomats and political analysts said that such was Dehaene's single-minded single currency ambition that the coalition would cling on until that decision was made.

"The PS will stay on at least until it has been decided who will be members of the Euro," a source close to the government said. "Once that is known the glue keeping the coalition together will weaken considerably."
The Liberals -- the main opposition parties -- have suggested that they simply replace the Socialists in the coalition, thereby avoiding early elections.

But Dehaene, aware that it would be taken as a sign of weakness by the money markets which would not hesitate to attack the franc and therefore ruin Belgium's chances of being in the vanguard of those joining the euro, has rejected the proposal.
The franc has already come under light but sustained pressure because of the political woes.
At the same time the PS would fight tooth and nail against such a swap.

It has been party to numerous tough decisions in areas such as pensions, welfare cuts and wage curbs that have been forced on the government by its efforts to cut its massive debts on the path to the single currency.

In order to become credible in opposition, the PS would have to start attacking the policies it had been partly responsible for -- a political backflip that in its weakened state the party would have considerable difficulty making, diplomats said. ($ = 34.82 Belgian Francs)
